name: Facial feedback
statement: The arrangement of your own face feeds back into how you feel, so holding a smile makes things seem funnier even when you did not smile because of them.
meaning: The hypothesis reverses the usual direction. Instead of amusement producing a smile, the smile is held to produce some of the amusement. What made the idea testable was a way to arrange someone's face without telling them why: give them a pen to hold in their mouth. Held in the teeth it recruits the muscles of a smile, held in the lips it prevents one, and the participant thinks the study is about writing with your mouth. Any difference in how funny they find a cartoon afterwards cannot be explained by their knowing what expression they were making.

origin.who: Fritz Strack, Leonard L. Martin and Sabine Stepper
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Their paper is titled "Inhibiting and facilitating conditions of the human smile: A nonobtrusive test of the facial feedback hypothesis". The replicators describe it as commonly discussed in introductory psychology courses and textbooks, and counted 1,370 Google Scholar citations in May 2016.

evidence: The 1988 paper reports two studies, and the famous number comes from the first. Study 1 tested 92 undergraduates at the University of Illinois in three conditions: pen in the teeth, pen in the lips, pen in the nondominant hand. Mean funniness ratings were 5.14 for teeth, 4.77 for the hand and 4.32 for the lips, on a scale from 0 to 9, so the quoted gap of 0.82 is the distance between the two extremes of a three-condition design. The test the authors report for it is a linear contrast across all three, t(89) = 1.85, p = .03, a directional result close to the conventional threshold. Study 2 tested 83 students at Mannheim University and split the humour response in two. There the pen left funniness ratings alone, with all ps above .20, and moved only the separate amusement rating, which ran 6.43 in the teeth condition against 5.40 in the lips condition, t(75) = 1.78. The replication report gives that gap as 1.03. The authors also note that the group codings for Study 1 were lost through a clerical oversight. The replicators state that the study had not been replicated directly using the same design and the same dependent variable, and searches of Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and Europe PMC in August 2026 found no earlier direct repeat.

replication.headline: Two preregistered multi-lab tests found nothing for the pen, while smaller studies run without a camera, or in a classroom, still get the original effect.
replication.detail: The Registered Replication Report followed one vetted protocol at every site. Its 17 laboratories tested 2,533 people and analysed 1,894, the gap being strict exclusions. Where the original found a 0.82-unit gap on its ten-point scale, the random-effects meta-analysis found 0.03 units, with a 95% confidence interval from -0.11 to 0.16. Nine of the 17 site results pointed in the predicted direction, and none produced a gap as large as 0.82. The target was Study 1 of Strack and colleagues, with three declared changes: the rating wording came from their Study 2, the nondominant-hand condition was dropped, and instructions were delivered by video. A second multi-lab test in 2022, the Many Smiles Collaboration, added a pen-in-mouth arm alongside two other manipulations. It collected 3,878 participants from 26 research groups spanning 19 countries and kept 1,504 for the primary analyses, and the pen arm moved self-reported happiness by 0.04 points, 95% confidence interval -0.07 to 0.15, with Bayes factors favouring the null. Two smaller studies point the other way, and they are the reason this entry is filed as mixed rather than failed. Every laboratory in the 2016 report ran a video camera on the participant, which Noah, Schul and Mayo say the 1988 study did not. They tested that in 2018 on 200 Hebrew-speaking students, 166 of whom entered the analysis, and found the teeth-lips gap in the no-camera rooms (5.75 against 4.92, t(162) = 2.48, p = .01) and nothing in the camera rooms (5.21 against 5.15, p = .85). The interaction their claim rests on came out at t(162) = 1.64, p = .051 one-tailed, which they call marginally significant and greatly underpowered. Marsh, Rhoads and Ryan then ran the pen task on more than 400 undergraduates across nine semesters of a classroom demonstration and report evidence for the effect at a magnitude that overlapped the original.

study.cite: Wagenmakers, E.-J., Beek, T., Dijkhoff, L., et al. (2016). Registered Replication Report: Strack, Martin, & Stepper (1988). Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(6), 917-928.

limits: No confidence interval for the 0.82 gap was found in the 1988 paper. The copy read here is a scan whose tables did not render, so any interval may sit in its Table 1. The replication report does supply one for the original, drawn in the forest plot and computed by the replicators from the summary statistics under an assumption of homogeneous variance and homogeneous sample size, and its numeric bounds are not printed in the article text. Both headline figures are on the study's own rating scale rather than standardised, which is how both papers report them. The 2022 result is on a different measure again, self-reported happiness from 1 to 7, so it cannot be lined up against the 0.82. That study ran entirely online because covid stopped in-person collection, and it excluded 46% of participants for showing awareness of the hypothesis. Strack, replying in the same issue as the 2016 report, put its exclusion rate at 24% and noted that the 14 labs recruiting from psychology subject pools averaged d = -0.03 against d = 0.16 for the three that did not, t(15) = 2.35, p = .033, an analysis he ran after seeing the data. Marsh, Rhoads and Ryan sits behind a paywall: its sample of over 400 and its conclusion are taken from the abstract at PubMed, and no effect size from it appears here.
misreadings: The result is often stated as proof that facial expressions have no effect on emotion. It is narrower than that. What failed is one specific demonstration at the size it originally reported, and a hypothesis is not one experiment. Coles, Larsen and Lench pooled 286 effect sizes from 138 studies in 2019 and put the overall effect of facial feedback on self-reported affect at d = 0.20, 95% confidence interval 0.14 to 0.26, small and heterogeneous. Their subgroup for emotional experience alone gives d = 0.17, 0.11 to 0.23. The Many Smiles Collaboration found that posing a happy expression raised self-reported happiness by 0.31 points on a one-to-seven scale, 95% confidence interval 0.21 to 0.40, with the mimicry task at 0.49 and the voluntary facial action task at 0.40 while the pen task returned 0.04. So the hypothesis has support and the pen does not carry it. The camera is treated as a settled explanation for the failure, and it is not. Coles and colleagues found little sign of it, with d = 0.17 for participants aware of video recording against d = 0.23 for those unaware, and a moderator coefficient of -0.06, 95% confidence interval -0.20 to 0.07. Phaf and Rotteveel repartitioned that same dataset in 2023 by whether anyone else was in the room, and got d = 0.444 for unobtrusive studies with a social context against d = 0.099 without, while calling their analysis exploratory and post hoc. The pen study is also still taught as an established result, which is the more common error. Embodied cognition, entry 54, covers the wider programme this belongs to, and power posing, entry 155, is the postural version of the same argument.
